overview: Lineworkers shrug off the AI Plateau and stay mostly calm under Steady Disruption, sure that no robot will climb an icy pole soon and that AI needs more power lines, not fewer. AGI by 2028 is the shock: worry jumps to 3.5 out of 5, and most cut spending, save hard and lean on family, church, the union or the state. With five or ten years' warning they turn to saving and retraining, and in every scenario adaptable lineworkers with savings stay calmest while those who resist change and have little put by worry most.

S0.headline: Nearly every lineworker stays calm and carries on as before, seeing AI as a handy helper for reports and rulebooks while the real work stays up the pole.

whatTheyDo.text: All of them keep working as now, taking storm overtime and weekend standby to chip away at a mortgage, a van loan or the kids' school costs.
Almost four in ten keep using AI for the dull bits, like incident reports, job packs, specs and rule changes, and some add a drone licence or a short course.
About three in ten keep putting money aside, often for a wedding, a house deposit or a few more months of cover, usually out of overtime pay.
About one in eight push harder through the union, for example joining the bargaining committee or pressing for better winter staffing and a fairer regional rate.
About one in ten grow something on the side, such as weekend drone inspections for solar farms, private jobs connecting farm sheds, or honey and photography.

S0.whatTheySay: Most say they're not surprised and that AI is a useful tool, like a calculator or a satnav. Many add that it can't change a crossarm in sideways rain, and some point out that the AI boom still meant building more lines.
S0.whatTheyThink: Privately most are relieved that their job, pay and plans stay on track until they finish or retire. Several say their real worries never had anything to do with robots: thin savings, rent, a parent's care costs, or a depot shrinking to save money.
S0.howTheyFeel: Calm and settled, like a storm warning that turns out to be drizzle. A few keen users feel a little let down.

differences.text: Worry is the same for everyone, but adaptive lineworkers keep learning AI tools far more (91%) than steady ones (22%), and none of the resistant ones do.
Progressive lineworkers are the only ones who push through the union (40%), while traditional ones lean more on side income (22%).
Those with thin savings look for side income more (19%) than those with strong savings (2%), who are the ones most likely to invest (12%).

quotes.name: Yusuf Okafor
quotes.text: If AI is mostly hype, we still built the lines for it.

quotes.name: Daria Usman
quotes.text: The robot can come and change a crossarm in sideways rain and then we'll talk.

quotes.name: Aaron Fischer
quotes.text: The kids' school shoes come out of the overtime from storm callouts, so I'm the only lineworker I know who prays for bad weather.

S1.headline: Lineworkers split between calm and a little uneasy, and most decide to learn the new kit, often once it's proven on another crew, rather than wait to be left behind.

whatTheyDo.text: Six in ten set out to learn the new tools, often by asking to join a drone inspection trial or a robot arm trial, or by signing up once a couple of other crews have used them.
About a third keep doing the job as before, taking the overtime and learning new gadgets only when they're told to.
About a third save a bit harder just in case, for example an extra hundred a month or skipping a motorbike or a phone upgrade.
About a third turn to the union, pushing for a written deal on paid training, crew sizes and no cuts before any new tech reaches the crews.
About a third take a course, most often a commercial drone licence, which some pay for themselves, or evening classes in robotics or grid sensors.

S1.whatTheySay: Most take a practical line: let's see what the tools really do, and people should learn them rather than panic. Many add that AI needs power and power needs lines, and the union voices want workers at the table before the machines arrive.
S1.whatTheyThink: Privately many think climbing and live-line work will stay human longest, because mistakes kill people. The worry sits with those who are slow with tablets, older workers who cost the most, and young apprentices who might never get a full career.
S1.howTheyFeel: Calm or mildly uneasy, like a new noise from the truck. Those who like the tech feel a bit excited that the job is growing their way.

differences.text: Worry falls from 2.0 among resistant lineworkers to 1.0 among adaptive ones. Resistant ones mostly keep going (63%) and wait and see (57%), while adaptive ones learn the tools (94%), retrain (62%) and start side income (43%).
Almost all progressive lineworkers take collective action (94%), against hardly any others. Traditional ones keep going (51%) and look for side income (36%) instead.
Worry falls from 1.7 for those with thin savings to 1.4 for those with strong savings.

quotes.name: Karl Costa
quotes.text: All this AI needs power, and power needs lines, and my crew builds lines.

quotes.name: Jade Quinn
quotes.text: If a drone does the looking and a computer does the deciding, then what am I, the driver?

quotes.name: Dana Gupta
quotes.text: I'd keep my paper notebook in my jacket. Thirty-one years of fault notes are in there, and that notebook's never crashed.

S2.headline: Most lineworkers are anxious or alarmed, cutting spending to the bone and leaning on family, church, the union or the state, because two years leaves no time to adjust.

whatTheyDo.text: Seven in ten cut back hard, often in the first week, keeping only the mortgage, food, power and fuel and dropping holidays, a new truck or the kids' clubs.
About half put every spare amount into savings, for example cancelling a family trip or shrinking a wedding to stretch a few months of cover into eight.
Over four in ten look for help, such as moving in with parents or a grown child, asking the church or a brother for support, or signing up for government help the day they're laid off.
Three in ten push the union for a redundancy deal, a hold on layoffs, or rules that keep human crews alongside the robots.
About a quarter turn to politics, joining protests for an income guarantee, writing to their representative, or campaigning for a public share of the machines.

S2.whatTheySay: Most say it's far too fast for companies or government to handle well, and that someone has to keep people afloat while it settles. Some still want proper work rather than handouts, and the keenest say people should learn the robots and move.
S2.whatTheyThink: Privately many think their job and their partner's could both be gone within two years, with savings that would run out fast. Many think about their kids, their town or the young apprentices. A few with tech skills hope to land on a robot crew but doubt it would last.
S2.howTheyFeel: Anxious or alarmed, often lying awake doing the sums. A few feel panicked, like standing under a rotten pole with nowhere to step.

differences.text: Worry rises from 3.0 for lineworkers with strong savings to 3.9 for those with thin savings, who mostly cut spending (90%) and seek support (72%) and can hardly save at all (7%).

Worry rises from 2.8 among adaptive lineworkers to 4.0 among resistant ones. Resistant ones cut spending (89%) and seek support (74%), while adaptive ones change jobs (53%), automate (38%) and invest (36%).
Progressive lineworkers organise (90% take collective action) and turn to politics (73%), while traditional ones lean on family and church (63% seek support) and side income (43%).
Late-career lineworkers worry a little less (3.3) and more than a third of them retire early (38%), something no one early in their career does.

quotes.name: Adam Chen
quotes.text: Like standing under a pole you know is rotten at the base. You can hear it creak and there's nowhere to step to.

quotes.name: Nora Novak
quotes.text: I'd be doing the maths on the ceiling at two in the morning, and the maths doesn't work.

quotes.name: Ivan Lopez
quotes.text: I'd tell him to learn the robots before they learn him.

S3.headline: Lineworkers still worry, but five years feels like time for a plan: most save hard and more than half start training for what comes next.

whatTheyDo.text: Three in four build up savings, for example overpaying the mortgage, putting aside a hundred a month from overtime or aiming for six to nine months of cover.
More than half train for something new, such as an evening robotics course, a drone licence, a safety inspector certificate or a house-wiring licence.
Three in ten grow a second income, like weekend fence work, egg and garden sales, or part-time work at a family garage once line work dries up.
About a quarter work through the union, standing as a steward for the first time or pushing for a bridge payment that carries older workers to their pension.
About a quarter learn the new equipment, often once the first robot crews have it working, and aim for a role checking or supervising the robots.

S3.whatTheySay: Most say five years is enough to get ready if people start now, and that companies, unions and government should set up training and fair notice early. Some still want to see a robot fix a line in the mud before they believe it.
S3.whatTheyThink: Privately many think the ending is the same as with two years, but the landing is softer. Older lineworkers hope to reach retirement first, while younger ones see time to qualify and move into maintaining or supervising the robots.
S3.howTheyFeel: Mostly anxious or uneasy, a slow daily weight rather than a punch, but with a path in sight.

differences.text: Worry falls from 3.1 among resistant lineworkers to 1.7 among adaptive ones. Resistant ones mostly save (95%) and hardly retrain (9%), while adaptive ones retrain (79%), start side income (51%) and invest (49%).
Worry falls from 2.9 for thin savings to 2.1 for strong savings. Nearly everyone with a thin cushion saves (95%), while those with a strong one invest more (36%).
Progressive lineworkers organise (77% take collective action), while traditional ones build side income (58%) and invest (40%).
Late-career lineworkers worry least (2.3) and are the most likely to just keep going (31%), as many expect to retire before it arrives.

quotes.name: Emeka Larsen
quotes.text: In two years I'm a man looking for work. In five I could be a man offering it.

quotes.name: Dana Rossi
quotes.text: Five years doesn't change where I end up, it changes how hard I land.

quotes.name: Dana Diaz
quotes.text: Every demo I've ever seen is on a sunny day in a car park. Show me one in February on a rotten pole.

S4.headline: With ten years' warning most lineworkers are calm or only a little uneasy, so they keep working, save steadily and put their families first.

whatTheyDo.text: Almost six in ten carry on with their plans, finishing the apprenticeship, making foreman or working to retirement, and wait a few years to see what's real.
About half save steadily, for example a fixed amount every month or extra off the mortgage so the house is nearly theirs when it arrives.
Almost half plan around family, such as steering their children towards a trade or course that won't vanish, or helping a son-in-law onto the new kit early.
Almost four in ten retrain at a calmer pace, often starting a robotics, protection or inspector course in year three or four.
About a quarter slowly build something of their own, like a drone survey or firewood business, and buy robots for it once prices fall.

S4.whatTheySay: Most say ten years is plenty of time if people don't waste it, so companies should train people now and nobody should end up on the scrap heap. Some warn that ten years can easily turn into two if nobody organises.
S4.whatTheyThink: Privately many feel it's manageable. Older lineworkers expect to be retired and worry for younger crew and grandchildren, while some in their twenties find it cruel to spend their best years on a trade that's ending.
S4.howTheyFeel: Calm or uneasy, a background worry like a long winter you know is coming, and for some even hopeful.

differences.text: Worry falls from 2.3 among resistant lineworkers to 1.1 among adaptive ones. Resistant ones mostly keep going (81%) and save (75%), while adaptive ones invest (54%) and build side income (48%).
Late-career lineworkers worry least (1.4) and nearly all keep going (90%). Mid-career ones worry most (1.9) and focus on family plans (68%), while early-career ones retrain more (49%).
Progressive lineworkers lean on collective action (59%) and politics (51%), while traditional ones put family plans first (65%).
Worry falls from 1.9 for thin savings to 1.5 for strong savings, and those with a thin cushion save far more (81% against 37%).

quotes.name: Nora Novak
quotes.text: Ten years sounds like loads of time, and that's exactly how you end up at thirty-six with nothing done.

quotes.name: Jade Farah
quotes.text: Being the last one out on Route 9 isn't the worst thing; somebody's got to turn the lights off.

quotes.name: Fatima Okafor
quotes.text: With ten years' warning, I'm not the one being replaced, I'm the one teaching the replacement where the old cables are buried.
